mcqs.q: A granuloma is composed predominantly of:
opts: Epithelioid cells (modified macrophages) rimmed by lymphocytes
mcqs.explain: A granuloma is a tiny lesion of epithelioid cells (modified macrophages) rimmed by lymphocytes, with giant cells, fibrosis and necrosis.

mcqs.q: Tuberculosis is the classic example of:
mcqs.explain: TB is the classic chronic granulomatous disease, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

mcqs.q: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a:
mcqs.explain: M. tuberculosis is a strict aerobe and an acid-fast bacillus (rod).

mcqs.q: Mycobacterium bovis characteristically causes which form of TB?
mcqs.explain: M. bovis (e.g. from unpasteurised milk) causes oropharyngeal and intestinal tuberculosis.

mcqs.q: Which factor predisposes to tuberculosis?
opts: Malnutrition, crowding, diabetes, alcoholism or AIDS
mcqs.explain: Predisposing factors include malnutrition, poverty, crowding, uncontrolled diabetes, alcoholism and immunocompromise (AIDS).

mcqs.q: The main organ affected in TB, and its route of spread, are:
opts: The lung; airborne droplets from coughing/sneezing
mcqs.explain: The lung is the main organ; MBT is carried on airborne droplets (coughing/sneezing) and enters via the airway.

mcqs.q: The Mantoux (tuberculin) test uses:
opts: 0.1 cc of 5 TU of purified protein derivative (PPD), read at 48–72 h
An oral tablet read at 1 hour
A blood culture read at 2 weeks
mcqs.explain: The Mantoux test injects 0.1 cc of 5 TU PPD intradermally; the skin is read at 48–72 h for induration and redness.

mcqs.q: A Mantoux test is considered POSITIVE when the induration is:
mcqs.explain: Induration ≥10 mm = positive; 5–9 mm = inconclusive; <5 mm = negative.

mcqs.q: Primary tuberculosis is characterised by the:
opts: Ghon's (primary) complex: a primary focus plus an enlarged hilar lymph node
mcqs.explain: Primary (childhood) TB forms Ghon's complex: a 1–2 cm subpleural primary focus plus an enlarged hilar lymph node.

mcqs.q: Primary tuberculosis affects a host who is:
opts: Not previously infected or immunized, and is usually asymptomatic
mcqs.explain: Primary TB is the first infection of a non-immune host; it is usually an asymptomatic focus (Ghon's complex).

mcqs.q: Secondary (post-primary) tuberculosis classically occurs at the lung APEX because:
opts: The high oxygen tension there favours the aerobic bacillus (causing cavitation)
The apex has the most blood supply
mcqs.explain: Secondary TB occurs at the apex because the high O₂ tension favours the aerobic MBT, leading to cavitation; it is the most infectious form.

mcqs.q: Which form of TB is the MOST infectious to others?
mcqs.explain: Secondary TB (with cavitation) is the most commonly infective to other individuals.

mcqs.q: Miliary tuberculosis is characterised by:
opts: Disseminated millet-seed-sized (1 mm) lesions in immunocompromised hosts
mcqs.explain: Miliary (tertiary) TB occurs when immunity is suppressed; the bacilli spread through the circulation, producing 1 mm millet-seed lesions in many organs.

mcqs.q: The clinical features of ACTIVE (secondary) TB include:
opts: Fever, night sweats, weight loss and a productive cough with blood-stained sputum
mcqs.explain: Active secondary TB causes intermittent fever, night sweats, weight loss, loss of appetite and a productive cough with blood-stained sputum.

mcqs.q: Actinomycosis is caused by:
opts: Actinomyces israelii — a filamentous, branched, gram-positive anaerobe
mcqs.explain: Actinomycosis is a chronic suppurative disease caused by Actinomyces israelii, a filamentous, branched, gram-positive anaerobe (an oral commensal).

mcqs.q: Actinomycosis infection is:
mcqs.explain: Actinomyces is a commensal of the oral cavity, gut and vagina; infection is always endogenous, not transmitted person-to-person.

mcqs.q: The COMMONEST form of actinomycosis (and best prognosis) is:
mcqs.explain: Cervicofacial actinomycosis is the commonest form (~60%) with the best prognosis.

mcqs.q: Cervicofacial actinomycosis typically enters through:
opts: Carious teeth, periodontal disease or trauma after tooth extraction
mcqs.explain: The infection enters from tonsils, carious teeth, periodontal disease or trauma following tooth extraction.

mcqs.q: The firm swelling of cervicofacial actinomycosis in the lower jaw is called:
mcqs.explain: Cervicofacial actinomycosis produces a firm swelling of the lower jaw — the classic 'lumpy jaw' — which breaks down into abscesses and sinuses.

mcqs.q: The discharging pus of actinomycosis characteristically contains:
mcqs.explain: The pus contains typical tiny yellow 'sulfur granules', which are colonies of Actinomyces.

mcqs.q: Thoracic and abdominal actinomycosis (~30%) usually arise from:
opts: Aspiration from the oral cavity or extension of abdominal/hepatic lesions
mcqs.explain: Thoracic and abdominal actinomycosis result from aspiration of the organism from the oral cavity or local extension of abdominal/hepatic disease.

mcqs.q: The central necrosis in a tuberculous granuloma is described as:
mcqs.explain: Tuberculous granulomas show central caseation (cheese-like) necrosis.

mcqs.q: Catching tuberculosis involves which two stages?
opts: First becoming infected, then the infection progressing to disease
mcqs.explain: The process has two stages: a person must first become infected, and then the infection has to progress to disease.

saqs.q: Define a granuloma and name the organism causing TB.
saqs.a: A tiny lesion of epithelioid cells (modified macrophages) rimmed by lymphocytes, with giant cells/fibrosis/necrosis. TB is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (acid-fast aerobe).

saqs.q: Describe the Mantoux test and its interpretation.
saqs.a: 0.1 cc of 5 TU PPD intradermally; read at 48–72 h. ≥10 mm = positive, 5–9 mm inconclusive, <5 mm negative.
The lesion of primary TB: a primary (Ghon) focus (1–2 cm subpleural consolidation) plus an enlarged hilar lymph node.

saqs.q: Differentiate primary, secondary and miliary TB.
saqs.a: Primary: Ghon's complex, childhood, asymptomatic. Secondary: reactivation, apical cavitation, most infective. Miliary: disseminated millet-seed lesions in immunocompromised.

saqs.q: Define actinomycosis and its causative organism.
saqs.a: A chronic suppurative disease caused by Actinomyces israelii (filamentous, branched, gram-positive anaerobe), an oral commensal — always endogenous.
Commonest form (~60%); enters via carious teeth/extraction → firm 'lumpy jaw' → abscesses & sinuses discharging yellow sulfur granules.

saqs.q: List the clinical features of active (secondary) TB.
saqs.a: Intermittent fever, night sweats, weight loss, loss of appetite, productive cough with blood-stained sputum.
